question: Two numbers whose sum is \(6\) and the absolute value of whose difference is \(8\) are roots of the equation:
solution:
Call the larger number \(u\) and the smaller \(v\). Ordering them turns the absolute difference into \(u-v=8\), so
\[
u+v=6,\qquad u-v=8.
\]
Adding these equations eliminates \(v\): \(2u=14\), giving \(u=7\). Then \(v=6-7=-1\). Thus the pair is determined up to order.

To build an equation with these roots, use one factor that vanishes at each number:
\[
(x-7)(x+1)=0.
\]
A product is zero exactly when at least one factor is zero, so this equation has precisely the required roots. Expanding gives
\[
(x-7)(x+1)=x^2-6x-7.
\]
The required equation is \(x^2-6x-7=0\), choice B.

After eliminating one unknown the procedure solves a one-variable linear equation; only this solving component is claimed.
Substitution introduces the reduction-to-one-variable idea, but adding equations to cancel an unknown is justified independently by equality operations.

The source expressly permits an area interpretation of the perfect-square identity; polynomial multiplication is one derivation, not the only route to the stated formula-use criteria.
A discriminant check guards real-root assumptions in parameter questions. A problem that already gives real roots can use Vieta's relations directly, so this is useful preparation.
